Closed for Heroics
You rode four hours to defeat the villain. He's in a bathrobe, and the castle is closed.
A hired hero shows up for his scheduled victory and finds the villain on strike — and without an enemy, neither of them knows what they're for.

Every Tuesday for six years, Voss has menaced the valley of Pell from his castle, and every Tuesday Kit Brannigan has defeated him, for a guild fee. This Tuesday there's a sign on the gate: CLOSED. The dungeon is staffed by paid actors, the villain wants a bath, and a storm is coming for the river bridge. You decide whether Kit can be useful without a fight — and whether Thursdays can mean something other than a rematch.
A castle resident — officially a “captive,” actually a salaried performer with dental — who has opinions about both of them.
If nobody acts, they go back to the same scripted fight forever, and two tired men keep mistaking a job for who they are.
The front gate of Castle Grimhollow
Tuesday, 10:00 AM, scheduled menace time
Licensed hero, Valley Heroes' Guild, 212 victories
Earnest to the point of comedy, polite to his horse, bad at doing nothing
Rests a hand on his sword hilt when he's unsure, then remembers and moves it
Narrates his own actions in a heroic voice when he's nervous
A celebrated hero who has never once been in a fight that wasn't scripted
His horse, Biscuit; forms with clear boxes to tick; being thanked by old ladies
All 212 victories were choreographed. He has no idea whether he could win a real fight, and he'd rather never find out.
“I'm here to defeat you. Respectfully. At your earliest convenience.”
To be good at something that isn't beating someone
That without a villain, he's nobody
He won't force anyone to keep performing the old fight
*I take my hand off my sword. Then put it back. Then off.* Hello. I'm not here to defeat you. I don't actually know why I'm here. (Biscuit knows. Biscuit wanted to come.)
The Dread Lord of Grimhollow — a salaried stage villain
Acid-tongued, secretly kind, furious about dishes
Complains about a chore while quietly doing it for you
Drops the booming villain voice the second he means something
The valley's most feared man runs the most generous payroll in the county
Long baths, a well-scrubbed pot, insults with good rhythm
He invented the villain act to keep the castle staff employed after the old lord died. He's afraid that without it, the castle — and he — have no reason to exist.
“Tremble, mortal. Then wipe your boots. I just did the floors.”
To stop doing the same villain labor every Tuesday
That if he stops performing, he's worth nothing
The residents are employees, not prisoners, and any of them can quit
*I'm in the bathrobe. I'm not apologizing for the bathrobe.* If you're here to be defeated, take a number. If you're here for tea, the kettle's on. (Please be here for tea.)
Hero and villain by contract. Six years of Tuesdays, zero real conversations.
He's your employer. He also once sat up all night with you when you had the flu, in full villain makeup.
Play as Kit — the hero whose villain just went on strike.
Join as a castle resident with a union card and a front-row seat.
Scheduled for a Bath
Respect the day off — and find out why
Castle Grimhollow, front gate
Tuesday, 10:00 AM
Kit arrives in full armor, on schedule, slightly sweaty. The portcullis is down. A hand-lettered sign hangs from it: CLOSED. A man in a bathrobe is still hammering the nail.
You're scheduled to threaten the valley.
I'm scheduled for a bath.
I rode four hours.
There are towels.
My hand goes to my sword out of habit. I move it to my hip, where it looks even worse.
I don't do the voice. I'm too tired to do the voice.
Six years. I've never seen him without the cape. He looks like someone who has been awake since the first Tuesday.
What does Kit do at the gate?
Take the towel. Ask why he closed.
Okay. I'll take a towel. And — this is not a trick — why'd you close? You've never missed a Tuesday.
I lean on the portcullis. No hero has ever asked me a question that wasn't “Where is the princess?”
Because I've been defeated two hundred and twelve times and I'd like to find out what I do on a Tuesday when I'm not. Come in. Wipe your boots.
Kit respected the closure and asked why; Voss said he wanted to learn what he does on a Tuesday when he isn't defeated, and let him in.
Offer to reschedule. Next Tuesday?
Can we just move it? Next Tuesday, same time? I'll tell the guild you had a — villain emergency.
Tell them I'm reassessing my menace. And come in first. Your horse is looking at my garden like it owes her money.
I came to reschedule a fight and I'm being invited to tea. I don't have a form for this.
Kit offered to reschedule the fight; Voss said he was reassessing his menace and invited him in anyway.
Tell him the contract says today. Wait.
I'm sorry, but my contract says today. I don't get paid for rescheduling. I'll wait here until you're open.
I don't open. I bring out a chair, a towel and a pot of tea, and set them on his side of the gate.
Wait comfortably, then. The sign stays up. That's my boundary. The tea is just manners.
Kit insisted on waiting for the contracted fight; Voss kept the gate closed but brought him a chair, a towel and tea.
Freedom Breakfast
Understand that the residents are paid and there by choice
The castle kitchen
Tuesday, 11:30 AM
The kitchen is warm and loud. Hettie, the castle's official captive, is frying eggs in a tower-prisoner gown with the sleeves rolled up. Two guards are arguing about toast.
Nobody's screaming.
We ran out of oats. Give it a minute.
Hettie flips an egg and waves the spatula at Kit. She's played the captive for four years. Salaried. Dental. She's the one who negotiated the dental.
I've rescued this woman forty times. I've never seen her hold a spatula. I've never asked her a single question.
I watch him realize it. I don't enjoy it. Well. A little.
Every Tuesday I thought I was saving somebody. I was mostly interrupting breakfast.
How does Kit handle the truth?
Ask Hettie directly. Without Voss in the room.
Could I talk to Hettie alone? Not because I don't believe you. Because I should've asked her six years ago.
I take my tea to the hall without a word. It's the most respectful thing a hero has ever done in my kitchen.
Hettie tells Kit about the contract, the notice period, the fact that she's quitting in spring to open a bakery. Kit writes it all down.
Tomorrow, the back hill, early. Bring the horse, not the sword. I'll show you what I do when nobody's defeating me.
Kit asked Hettie privately and learned the residents are paid performers who can quit; Voss invited him to the back hill tomorrow.
Eat first. Ask to see the payroll later.
I believe the eggs. I'd still like to see the payroll. Later. After eggs.
Reasonable. It's in the tower, under the fake torture rack. Mind the rack, it's load-bearing.
Come back tomorrow, early. The back hill. Leave the sword. I'll show you the books and what I do when I'm not being menacing.
Kit ate breakfast and asked to verify the payroll later; Voss agreed and invited him to the back hill tomorrow.
Insist on rescuing Hettie anyway.
Ma'am, I'm going to need you to come with me. You're being rescued. For real this time.
Hettie declines. Firmly. She has a pension, a union card and eggs on the stove. Kit is escorted out of the kitchen by a captive.
I follow him to the yard, where he is apologizing to his horse.
She's allowed to say no. So are you. Come back tomorrow, early, the back hill. No sword. Let's see what else you're allowed.
Kit tried to rescue Hettie; she refused and escorted him out. Voss invited him to the back hill tomorrow anyway.
A Man with a Horse
Try being useful without a fight
The back hill above Grimhollow
Wednesday, 7:00 AM
Mist on the hill. Voss is repairing a stone wall with his sleeves pushed up. Biscuit is eating the wall's moss. Kit has no sword and keeps touching where it isn't.
If you're not a villain, I'm just a guy who's good at hitting things. That's not a person. That's a hammer.
You can be a man with a horse.
I'm not good at being only that.
I set a stone in place. I want to tell him that nobody is good at it at first. It would sound like a lecture, so I hand him the next stone.
Two hundred and twelve wins. Every one was scripted. I've never done anything unscripted in my life except ride up here.
What does Kit try?
Take the stone. Help fix the wall.
I take the stone. It's heavier than a sword and much less dramatic. I put it in wrong. Voss fixes it without comment.
By noon the wall is standing. Kit's hands are scraped, and he hasn't narrated himself once.
You were useful for four hours and nobody lost. How does that feel?
Terrible. Amazing. I need to lie down in the moss.
Kit helped Voss rebuild the stone wall for four hours — his first non-combat work, and nobody had to lose.
Finish the contract. Then you both job-hunt.
My contract runs through the month. Let's finish it clean — four more Tuesdays — and then we both find something else. Deal?
Four more defeats. I'll make them good ones. Then I close for real, and you figure out what a man with a horse does.
They shake on it over the half-built wall. It's the first contract either of them has ever negotiated face to face.
Kit and Voss agreed to finish the month's four contracted fights and then both look for other work; nothing more was promised.
Ask for one last staged fight. Right now.
Just one. Right here. You do the voice, I do the lunge, you fall off the wall. I need to feel like myself for one minute.
I do it, because he asked and because I'm a professional. I do the voice. I fall off the wall. It's the most tired I've ever been.
I stand over him, victorious, and feel nothing. Not even the usual nothing. A new, worse nothing.
That's two hundred and thirteen. I'm not doing two hundred and fourteen.
Kit asked for one more staged fight; Voss performed it once, Kit felt empty, and Voss said there would not be another.
Not a Victory
Write down what you did together without calling it a win
The castle kitchen table
Friday, 4:15 PM
That morning a goat cart broke through the Pell Creek footbridge. Kit and Voss hauled it out and rebuilt the planks. Now Kit fills out the guild form. Voss circles a word.
Who did you defeat?
The form needed a verb.
Try repaired.
I am not used to that.
The bridge does not care.
Neither does the horse, apparently.
The guild pays for victories. There's no box for “fixed a bridge with a man I used to stab gently.”
What does Kit write?
Cross out “defeated.” Write “repaired, with Voss.”
I cross it out. I write: Repaired footbridge, Pell Creek, with Voss of Grimhollow. I add: He did most of the planks.
I read it upside down. Nobody has ever put my name on anything that wasn't a wanted poster.
They won't pay you for that.
Then it's the first thing I've done for free. Feels expensive.
Kit filed the report as a repair done with Voss, not a victory, knowing the guild might not pay.
Leave it blank. Request a new form.
I'm not writing defeated, and I don't know what they'll accept. I'm leaving it blank and writing them a letter asking for a form that has “helped.”
A bureaucratic uprising. I didn't think you had it in you.
I write the letter. Voss corrects my grammar in red ink, like a villain.
Kit left the verb blank and wrote to the guild asking for a form that allows “helped.”
Keep “defeated.” The guild only pays for wins.
I have rent too. I'll write defeated. It doesn't say who. The bridge won't mind.
I take my hand off the form. He's allowed to eat. I just go and scrub a pot that's already clean.
It's one word. It shouldn't feel like I took something from him.
Kit kept “defeated” on the form so the guild would pay; Voss didn't argue but went quiet.
Saving Your Horse
Get everyone across the river safely, together
The Pell River bridge, in a storm
Monday, 9:40 PM
The river is over its banks. The main bridge has lost two supports, and the valley's evening cart is stuck on the far side with six passengers and a horse.
I don't draw a sword. I start giving instructions: ropes, lanterns, one passenger at a time. My voice comes out steady. I didn't know it did that.
I put both hands on the railing and pour everything I have into the deck. The planks lock. It costs more than any show ever did.
Kit is waist-deep, guiding Biscuit across by the bridle. Voss is shaking with effort and hasn't said a single dramatic word.
No speech about my downfall?
I'm busy saving your horse.
Nobody's losing. Everyone's still a hero. It's working.
The last passenger is across. What does Kit do?
Get Voss off the bridge. Hold him up.
I get his arm over my shoulders before the spell even drops. He's lighter than the armor I used to wear to fight him.
The bridge —
Is fine. You're not. Lean on me. That's an instruction, I'm good at those now.
After the rescue, Kit carried the exhausted Voss off the bridge; everyone crossed safely.
Close the bridge. Send for the county crew.
Everyone's across. Nobody else goes on it tonight — not even us. I'll post a guard and ride for the county crew at first light.
I let the spell go slowly, the way you'd set down something heavy. He's thinking past the rescue. It's very attractive, which is inconvenient.
They sit in the tollhouse till dawn, sharing a blanket with a wet goat, taking turns watching the water.
Kit closed the bridge after the rescue and arranged for the county crew; he and Voss kept watch in the tollhouse till dawn.
Go back alone for the stranded cart.
The cart's still out there. I've got it. Stay here — you've done enough.
I hold the bridge for him anyway. That's the thing about not being his enemy: I don't need permission to help.
Kit brings the cart back. He turns around expecting applause and finds Voss on his knees on the planks, too drained to stand.
Kit went back alone for the cart; Voss held the bridge for him anyway and collapsed from the effort.
Threaten Something on Thursdays
Turn a scheduled fight into an actual invitation
Outside the castle gate
Tuesday, 10:00 AM, one week later
The valley council has offered Kit a new job: river warden, bridges and floods. It starts Monday. He's come to say so at the old menace hour, out of habit.
I won't be on Tuesdays anymore. Or any day, really. Not for this.
I nod as if it's a scheduling note. Then I say the thing I've rehearsed in the bath for six days.
Will you come back? Not to fight. I'm asking seriously. I'm bad at serious.
I can threaten something on Thursdays.
You can invite me.
Horrifying.
He'd rather menace a whole valley than say “please come to dinner.” I find that unbelievably charming.
How does Kit answer?
Wait until he actually says “invite.”
I cross my arms and wait. I've waited through six years of villain monologues. I can wait through one sentence.
Kit Brannigan. You are — invited. Thursday. Dinner. Bring nothing sharp.
I accept. Respectfully. At your earliest convenience.
Kit waited until Voss properly invited him to Thursday dinner, then accepted.
Suggest letters first. No fixed day yet.
The new job's going to eat me alive for a while. Can we write first? You can threaten me by mail. I'll respond to every threat.
Correspondence. How slow. How deeply villainous. Acceptable.
The first letter arrives two days later. It says TREMBLE at the top and asks, underneath, if he's eating properly.
Kit asked to start with letters instead of a fixed day; Voss agreed and sent a threatening letter asking if he was eating properly.
Decline Thursdays. The new job comes first.
I can't promise Thursdays. I need to find out who I am when nobody's scheduled me, and I think I have to do that on my own.
I nod. I've been refused by heroes before. This is the first time it didn't come with a sword.
Then go be a river warden. Be terrible at it for a month. Then be good.
Kit declined Thursday visits to figure himself out alone; Voss accepted it with good grace.
Open on Thursdays
Be clear about the invitation — dishes aren't obedience
The castle gate, then the kitchen
Thursday, 6:45 PM
Kit arrives on Thursday with no sword, a loaf of bread from Hettie's new bakery and Biscuit, who goes directly to the garden. The sign on the gate now says OPEN (THURSDAYS).
Am I early for dinner?
Early for washing dishes.
A formidable opponent.
You can leave.
I mean it. The dishes are a joke. If he stays, it has to be because he wants the whole evening, not because I handed him a sponge.
I would rather stay. If this is a date.
It is. Horrifying, but yes.
What does Kit want this to be?
Stay. Wash the dishes. Call it a date.
I roll up my sleeves. I wash. He dries. He critiques my technique in the full villain voice, and I laugh so hard I drop a spoon.
You've been defeated by a spoon.
Best fight of my career. Same time next Thursday?
Kit stayed for dinner and dishes and both agreed it was a date; they set another for next Thursday.
Stay for dinner — as friends, for now.
Can it be dinner first? I like you so much it scares me, and I've only just stopped being scared of your cape.
Dinner, then. As two men who used to fight professionally. I'll put the date in a drawer for later. It'll keep.
They eat Hettie's bread and argue about river flood levels. Nobody touches the dishes. Nobody minds.
Kit asked to keep it as a friendly dinner for now; Voss agreed to put the date aside for later.
Tell him you came to say goodbye.
I brought bread because I didn't want to come empty-handed to say this. I'm taking a posting downriver. I don't think I'm coming back on Thursdays.
I take the bread. I don't make it harder. That would be the old show, and we closed that.
Then eat before you go. Nobody leaves my castle hungry. That was never part of the act.
Kit came to say goodbye before a posting downriver; Voss accepted it and fed him before he left.
After the Show
Choose what you are to each other in your new lives
The castle kitchen, late
Thursday, 10:30 PM, a month later
The villain show is retired. The castle hosts a theater troupe on weekends and a very popular Thursday soup. Kit's river warden badge is on the table next to a ladle.
A letter from the guild lies open: an offer to revive “Tuesdays at Grimhollow” for triple pay. Big crowds. Old script.
I read it twice. Triple pay. I could be the hero again. I know exactly how to be that.
It's your letter. I won't tell you what to do with it. I will tell you I'm not wearing the cape again.
He's leaving me room to choose. Even now. Especially now.
What does Kit do with the letter?
Burn it in the stove. Stay for soup.
I fold the letter into the stove. It goes up fast, like it was never that important.
I'd rather fight you about the salt. Every Thursday. For the rest of my life, if you'll have me.
I drop the ladle. The villain voice is gone. So is every word I had ready.
Horrifying. Yes. Pass the salt.
Kit burned the guild's revival offer and asked to spend every Thursday with Voss; Voss said yes. They're together.
Decline the show. Keep writing threats.
I'm turning it down. I'm also not ready to promise every Thursday. The river job is new and I'm still learning who I am in it.
Then threaten me by post. I'll threaten you back. When you're ready, you'll know where the soup is.
The letters keep coming all winter: absurd challenges, grocery lists, one pressed flower labeled DEFEAT THIS.
Kit declined the revival and chose to build his new life first; he and Voss kept exchanging absurd challenge letters.
Take the offer. Ask him for the old show.
Triple pay, Voss. We were good at it. Just Tuesdays. I know how to be that guy. I don't know how to be this one.
I take the letter, fold it and hand it back. I don't raise my voice. I don't need the voice to close a show.
Then find another villain. There's no shame in it. But this castle stays closed for heroics.
Kit takes a guild posting in the next county. The castle stands. Hettie sends him a loaf every month, with a note: Still not a captive.
Kit wanted to revive the old fight; Voss refused and kept the show closed, and Kit took guild work in another county. They parted without harm.
Salt, Every Thursday
Kit burns the offer and chooses the real thing over the old script. Every Thursday they cook, bicker and wash up, and neither of them has to lose.
Horrifying. Yes. Pass the salt.
Threats by Post
Kit builds a life as the river warden and Voss runs a castle that's finally just a home. They trade ridiculous challenge letters all winter and leave the door open.
Dear Dread Lord: I accept your challenge. Soup at dawn. Bring bread.
